subsystems.name: Micro-agents
subsystems.role: the individual units, from a few nanometres to a few tens of micrometres across.
parts: rigid or flexible body (polymer, silica, metal)
surface coating for targeting and stealth

subsystems.name: Propulsion and actuation
subsystems.role: moves each unit through a fluid where viscosity dominates and simple paddling does not work.

subsystems.name: Local sensing and signalling
subsystems.role: lets units read their surroundings and leave chemical traces others can follow.

subsystems.name: Collective control
subsystems.role: turns thousands of individually dumb units into a coordinated mass.
parts: decentralised rule set (follow the concentration gradient)
external field coils or ultrasound array

subsystems.name: Power and payload
subsystems.role: supplies energy and delivers the therapeutic or repair action.
parts: chemical fuel or external energy field

subsystems.name: Safety and clearance
subsystems.role: must not be permanently left behind in the body.

buildSteps.title: Choose the size regime
buildSteps.detail: Below about 100 nm a unit cannot carry propulsion or payload; between 1 µm and 1 mm (about the scale of a human hair's width) magnetic steering and imaging work far better. Most real work sits in that micrometre band.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the bodies
buildSteps.detail: Micrometre units are made top-down by photolithography or two-photon polymerisation, then coated with a magnetic layer such as iron oxide; nanoparticles are made bottom-up by chemical precipitation and assembled into clusters.

buildSteps.title: Functionalise the surface
buildSteps.detail: Antibodies, peptides or enzymes are attached so units stick to tumour cells or damaged material and not to healthy tissue; a polymer coat delays immune clearance.

buildSteps.title: Add propulsion
buildSteps.detail: An external rotating or oscillating magnetic field or an ultrasound standing wave drives the swarm; some designs instead attach motile bacteria whose flagella provide thrust.

buildSteps.title: Program the swarm rules
buildSteps.detail: Each unit follows simple local rules — move up the chemical gradient, emit a signal when the local concentration passes a threshold, cluster when enough neighbours signal back. Borrowed from quorum sensing in bacteria and from stigmergy, the trail-following coordination seen in ants and termites.

buildSteps.title: Test in microfluidics
buildSteps.detail: Swarms are steered through channels and tissue-mimicking gels, with cameras tracking how many units reach the target and how tightly they cluster.

buildSteps.title: Test in animals
buildSteps.detail: Doses are injected into small animals; imaging tracks the swarm, and tissue is later examined for delivered drug and for harm.

buildSteps.title: Plan administration and removal
buildSteps.detail: For human use the route must be decided — injection into blood, a body cavity or directly into tissue — along with how the units are activated and how they break down or are retrieved.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture in quantity
buildSteps.detail: Producing billions of identical, sterile, quality-controlled units is a pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing problem that has not been solved at this scale.

prerequisites.why: micrometre-scale magnetic particles and swimmers can be made and steered; true machines with onboard logic at the nanoscale do not exist.
MRI and ultrasound can image a swarm as a blurred mass, but cannot yet resolve or steer individual units deep in tissue.
synthetic biologists have made bacteria talk to each other with quorum-sensing circuits, but transferring that control to synthetic robots is early.
there is no compact power source at nanoscale, so motion must come from external fields that weaken and blur with depth.
the body must excrete or break down every unit; non-degradable metal or polymer debris accumulating in organs is a blocking safety issue.

pathway.milestone: magnetically steered microrobot swarms demonstrated in lab fluids and in small animals for localised drug delivery
pathway.unlocks: proof that a field can herd thousands of units to a chosen spot.

pathway.milestone: engineered bacteria and biohybrid swimmers carrying genetic circuits that switch on only when the swarm reaches a tumour
pathway.unlocks: self-amplifying, chemically coordinated delivery without external tracking of every unit.

pathway.milestone: first-in-human trials of image-guided microrobot swarms for a single, well-localised condition
pathway.unlocks: real data on dosing, safety and clearance in people.

pathway.milestone: biodegradable, self-powered colonies that disperse on command
pathway.unlocks: routine targeted therapy — and, in industrial settings, materials that sense and repair their own cracks, though that regime is far less developed than the medical one.
